title: Evaluating Statistical Claims
subtitle: Identify bias, generalizability, causation vs. correlation, and valid conclusions from studies

sections.title: Four Questions for Every Statistical Claim
sections.content:
Every SAT question about a study or survey asks at least one of these four questions:

1. **Is the sample biased?** Does it represent the target population?
2. **How broadly can we generalize?** Who does the conclusion apply to?
3. **Causation or correlation?** Can we say one thing *caused* another?
4. **What is a valid conclusion?** Given what was studied, what can we say?

Learn to identify which question is being asked before looking at the answer choices.

sections.title: What Makes a Sample Biased?
sections.content:
A sample is **biased** when it systematically over-represents or under-represents part of the population, making results unreliable for the whole group.

**Common sources of bias:**
- **Self-selection:** people who choose to participate have different views than those who don't
- **Convenience sampling:** only surveying easily accessible people (students in one class, shoppers at one mall)
- **Undercoverage:** leaving out parts of the population (surveying only online users about internet access)
- **Leading questions:** question phrasing that nudges a particular answer

**Unbiased sampling:** randomly selecting from the full target population.

sections.title: Example: Dog Park Survey
sections.problem: A city wants to know if residents support converting a field to a dog park. The city council surveys 500 **dog owners**. The majority support it. Which is the best description of this survey's limitation?

steps.description: Target population = all city residents. Sample = dog owners only
Dog owners have a systematic reason to favor a dog park — they're not representative
steps.math: \text{Biased: overrepresents people who benefit from a dog park}

sections.answer: The survey is **biased** because it only includes dog owners, who are more likely to support the park than the general population.
sections.tip: Ask: 'Does the group being sampled have a systematic reason to respond differently from the whole population?' If yes → biased.

sections.title: Example: Voluntary Response Bias
sections.problem: A company posts an online survey asking customers to rate their service. 200 people respond. Should the company trust the results as representative of all customers?

steps.description: Only customers who feel strongly (very satisfied or very dissatisfied) tend to respond voluntarily

sections.answer: No — voluntary response bias means the results overrepresent extreme opinions. Silent customers who were merely satisfied are underrepresented.
sections.tip: Voluntary response (people who choose to respond) always biases toward strong opinions. This is a very common SAT trap.

sections.title: Type 2: Generalizability — Who Can the Results Apply To?
Conclusions Can Only Apply to the Population That Was Sampled
sections.content:
The conclusions from any study can be extended to, at most, the **population that the sample was drawn from** (the sampling frame).

**You cannot generalize beyond the sampling frame.** Even if the sample was perfectly random:
- Random sample from one school → can generalize to that school only
- Random sample from all California State Universities → can generalize to all CSU students
- Random sample from all U.S. universities → can generalize to all U.S. university students

**Common wrong answers on SAT:** "All high school students in the country..." when only one school was sampled.

sections.title: Example: What Is the Largest Population?
sections.problem: Researchers randomly selected history professors from the California State Universities. What is the largest population to which the results can be generalized?

steps.description: The sampling frame = history professors at California State Universities
steps.math: \text{Can generalize to: all history professors at all CSUs}

steps.description: Cannot generalize to all U.S. history professors — not all universities were included

sections.answer: All **history professors at California State Universities**
sections.tip: The 'largest population' question: always limit to the actual sampling frame — the group you actually sampled from.

sections.title: Example: School vs. District
sections.problem: 40 fourth-grade students were randomly selected from Lincoln Elementary School. 32 thought morning announcements were helpful. Can we generalize to: (A) all fourth-graders at Lincoln, (B) all fourth-graders in the district, or (C) all fourth-graders in the state?

steps.description: Sample is from Lincoln Elementary only
Can generalize only to Lincoln's 4th graders
steps.math: \text{Only (A) is valid. (B) and (C) go beyond the sampling frame.}

sections.answer: (A) All fourth-graders at Lincoln Elementary School. Options B and C exceed the sampling frame.
sections.tip: Each step up (school → district → state → country) requires a random sample from that larger population.

sections.title: Two Types of Studies — Different Conclusions
sections.content:
| Study type | How subjects are divided | What can be concluded |
|---|---|---|
| **Observational study** | Researchers observe without assigning treatment | Association/correlation only — NOT causation |
| **Randomized experiment** | Subjects are randomly assigned to treatment/control | Can conclude causation |

**The key question:** Were subjects **randomly assigned** to groups?
- YES → experiment → **causation possible**
- NO → observational → **correlation only**, not causation

**Why does random assignment matter?** It ensures the groups are similar in all background factors, so any difference in outcome must be due to the treatment.

sections.title: Example: Can We Conclude Causation?
sections.problem: A psychologist randomly assigned 35 students from one middle school to two groups: half played an educational math game, half didn't. Students who played the game scored higher on a fraction test. Can the psychologist conclude that the game CAUSED improved scores?

steps.description: Were subjects randomly assigned? YES — half were randomly assigned to play the game
Random assignment makes the groups initially similar, so the game is the only explanation
steps.math: \text{Causation can be concluded for this population}

steps.description: BUT: sample was from one middle school → can only generalize to students like those

sections.answer: Yes — causation CAN be concluded for the students in the study, because random assignment was used. But results generalize only to students similar to those at that school.
sections.tip: A study can conclude causation but have limited generalizability, or have broad generalizability but not conclude causation. These are separate questions.

sections.title: Example: Observational Study — No Causation
sections.problem: Researchers surveyed 1,000 adults and found that people who eat breakfast daily earn higher incomes on average. Can they conclude that eating breakfast CAUSES higher income?

steps.description: Researchers observed behavior — they did NOT randomly assign anyone to eat/skip breakfast
A third variable (e.g., lifestyle, schedule, economic background) could explain both breakfast habits and income

sections.answer: No — this is an observational study. We can only say eating breakfast and income are **associated**, not that breakfast causes higher income.
sections.tip: When there's no random assignment, there are always possible 'confounding variables' that could explain the association. That's why observational studies can't prove causation.

sections.title: Correct Language for Statistical Conclusions
sections.content:
**Correct:** 'approximately,' 'estimated,' 'it is plausible that,' 'on average'
**Incorrect:** 'exactly,' 'all,' 'certainly,' 'proves'

**Correct conclusions from a random sample:**
- Approximately X% of the [target population] has this characteristic
- It is estimated that Y individuals in the [target population] will...

**Wrong:**
- All members of the population... (a sample can't speak for every individual)
- Exactly 30%... (a sample gives an estimate, not a perfect figure)

sections.title: Example: Identify the Valid Conclusion
sections.problem:
1,000 adults were randomly selected from a large city. 78% reported being satisfied with air quality. Which conclusion is best supported?

A) Exactly 78% of all city residents are satisfied.
B) Approximately 78% of all city residents are satisfied.
C) All city residents are satisfied.
D) The results cannot be generalized to the city.

steps.description: The sample was RANDOM from the city → can generalize to city residents. Eliminates D
A sample gives an estimate, not an exact figure. 'Exactly' is too strong. Eliminates A
steps.math: \text{'Approximately' is correct language for sample estimates}

steps.description: C is way too strong — we can't say ALL residents are satisfied from 78% of a sample

sections.answer: B) Approximately 78% of all city residents are satisfied.
sections.tip: On SAT, eliminate any choice with 'all,' 'exactly,' or 'certainly.' Correct statistical conclusions use 'approximately' and apply only to the sampled population.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: **Biased sample:** systematically non-representative → conclusions don't generalize well
**Random sample:** can generalize to the population it was drawn from, but NO further
**Generalization scope:** limited to the sampling frame — always check who was actually sampled
**Causation:** only possible from a randomized experiment (random assignment to groups)
**Correlation:** all observational studies show only — not causation

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Generalizing beyond the sampling frame (e.g., all U.S. students from one school's data)
- Confusing 'random sample' (who is selected) with 'random assignment' (how subjects are divided into groups) — they are DIFFERENT
- Concluding causation from an observational study — the key question is 'were subjects randomly assigned?'
- Saying a biased sample produces NO information — it does give information about the biased group, just not the full population
- Accepting answer choices with 'all,' 'exactly,' or 'certainly' for sample-based conclusions

sat_tips: Ask 'who was sampled?' → conclusions apply ONLY to that group
Ask 'were subjects randomly assigned to treatment groups?' → if yes, causation is possible
Random sample (selecting subjects) ≠ random assignment (dividing into treatment groups) — know the difference
Correct language for sample conclusions: 'approximately,' 'estimated,' 'plausible' — never 'exactly' or 'all'
